questions.q: What was Cecilia Payne's central conclusion about the composition of stars in her 1925 thesis?
options: Stars are made mostly of iron and the same rocky metals as the Earth
Stars are overwhelmingly hydrogen, with helium next and everything else a trace
Stars are made of calcium and sodium, like the lines seen in the Sun
Each spectral class is made of a different dominant element
questions.explanation: Payne found that hydrogen was about a million times more abundant than the metals, with helium second — stars are an ocean of the two lightest elements, with everything else a thin contaminant. This overturned the assumption that stars were made of the same rocky, metallic stuff as the Earth.

questions.q: According to Payne's insight, what does the strength of a spectral line actually tell you?
options: The total amount of that element present in the star
The fraction of that element in the particular state that can absorb light, which is governed by temperature
The distance of the star from the Earth
The age of the star
questions.explanation: Line strength does not equal abundance. It reflects what fraction of an element's atoms happen to be in the one state able to absorb that light — and that fraction is set by temperature through ionisation, not by how much of the element is present.

questions.q: Why do type A stars like Sirius (around 10,000 degrees) show the strongest hydrogen absorption lines?
options: They contain far more hydrogen than cooler or hotter stars
Their temperature is just right to lift electrons to the second level to absorb, without stripping them off
Their atmospheres are denser, trapping more hydrogen
Hydrogen only forms at exactly 10,000 degrees
questions.explanation: To make the visible hydrogen lines the electron must sit in the second energy level. At about 10,000 degrees there is enough heat to populate that level but not enough to ionise the atoms away — the sweet spot. It is temperature, not extra hydrogen, that makes the lines blaze.

questions.q: Why do the very hottest O-type stars (30,000-40,000 degrees) show almost no visible hydrogen lines?
options: The hydrogen has fused entirely into helium
The heat strips the electron off the hydrogen, leaving a bare proton that cannot absorb light
Hydrogen sinks to the core at high temperatures
The light is too blue for hydrogen to absorb
questions.explanation: At O-star temperatures the hydrogen is ionised — the electron is torn clean off, leaving a bare proton with no electron to do any absorbing. The hydrogen is still there in abundance; it has simply been ionised into silence.

questions.q: Whose equation did Payne use to relate a star's temperature and electron pressure to the ionisation state of its atoms?
options: Henry Norris Russell's
Meghnad Saha's
Arthur Eddington's
Annie Jump Cannon's
questions.explanation: Saha's ionisation equation (1920-21) told her, for any element at a given temperature and electron pressure, what fraction of atoms were neutral, singly ionised, doubly ionised and so on. Feeding stellar temperatures into it let her correct line strengths for ionisation and recover true abundances.

questions.q: How does a stellar absorption spectrum arise, and how does it differ from a nebula's emission spectrum?
options: Both come from a thin gas with no background; the difference is only colour

Absorption lines are dark gaps bitten out of a continuous black-body rainbow from the hot dense core by the cooler atmosphere; emission lines are bright lines from a thin gas with no continuous source behind it
Absorption spectra come from cold stars and emission spectra from hot stars
Absorption lines are produced by the nucleus and emission lines by the electrons
questions.explanation: The dense interior radiates a continuous black-body spectrum; the cooler outer atmosphere absorbs specific colours, biting dark lines out of it. A thin glowing gas with nothing behind it instead radiates only at its own characteristic colours — bright emission lines on darkness. Same atoms and fingerprints; what differs is whether a hot continuous source shines through from behind.

questions.q: What did Payne's discovery reveal about the meaning of Annie Jump Cannon's O, B, A, F, G, K, M spectral sequence?
options: It is a sequence of changing chemical composition along the stars
It is a sequence of changing temperature, since the stars are made of essentially the same hydrogen and helium
It is a sequence of changing distance from the Earth
It is a sequence of changing stellar age
questions.explanation: Before Payne the sequence was a pattern with no physics behind it, assumed to be changing chemistry. After Payne it was clear the stars are chemical twins — overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium — and the sequence from blue-hot to red-cool is a thermometer, because different temperatures ionise different atoms into visibility.

questions.q: From memory: explain why line strength does not equal abundance, using hydrogen across cool, medium (A-type) and hot (O-type) stars.
keyPoints: A line is only produced if atoms are in the right state to absorb; that state depends on temperature.
Cool stars: hydrogen is present but too cold to lift electrons to the second level, so the lines are weak.
A-type (~10,000 degrees): the sweet spot — electrons reach the second level without being stripped, so the lines blaze.
O-type (30,000-40,000 degrees): hydrogen is ionised to bare protons, no electron to absorb, so the lines fade again — even though hydrogen is still abundant.
questions.explanation: If you connected the changing line strength to temperature-driven ionisation rather than changing amount of hydrogen, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: From memory: outline how Payne worked backwards from measured line strengths to the true abundance of each element in a star.
keyPoints: Read the star's temperature from its colour, calibrated against Cannon's spectral sequence.
Feed that temperature into Saha's equation to find what fraction of each element's atoms are in the state that produces its lines.
Compare that against the line strengths measured on the photographic plates.
Work back from observed line strength, through the temperature-dependent ionisation, to the true number of atoms — repeated across hundreds of spectra.
questions.explanation: The key chain is temperature -> Saha ionisation fraction -> compare to measured line strength -> true abundance. Recalling that loop earns Good or Easy.

questions.q: Explain how Payne's discovery that stars are mostly hydrogen made the Hertzsprung-Russell main sequence physically understandable. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: Before Payne the H-R diagram was an empirical pattern — stars plotted by brightness against temperature fall along a diagonal main sequence — that nobody could fully explain. Payne showed that nearly all stars are made of essentially the same fuel, overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium. This means the main sequence is the strip of stars quietly fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores, in equilibrium between gravity pulling in and radiation pressure pushing out. Where a star sits along the sequence is then set mainly by its mass (how much fuel it gathered), not by differing composition — so the diagram only makes sense once you know the fuel is hydrogen.

criteria.descriptor: States the H-R main sequence was an empirical pattern lacking a physical explanation before Payne.
Identifies that stars are essentially the same composition (mostly hydrogen and helium) and the main sequence is hydrogen-burning stars in gravity/radiation equilibrium.
Links position along the main sequence to mass/fuel rather than to differing chemistry.

questions.explanation: The crux is that a common hydrogen fuel turns the H-R diagram from a pattern into physics: the main sequence is hydrogen fusion, and mass sets a star's place on it.
